implementation_notes: `Data.define(:city)` (Ruby 3.2) builds value classes that expose no member writers, and Ruby 3.3 added `Data#with(**kwargs)`, which returns a shallow copy with the named members replaced - `person.with(home: person.home.with(city: "Berlin"))` - so the copy-with half of the pattern is in the standard library and the nesting stays explicit. For typed, validated data the dry-struct gem provides the same mechanics through `#new(changeset)` on an immutable struct. Neither gives a composable focus, so a path that must be stored and reused is hand-written (a getter/setter lambda pair or a small class); for the ordinary "change one field" case `with` is shorter.
code_sketch:
Address = Data.define(:city)
Person  = Data.define(:name, :home)

p = Person.new(name: "Ada", home: Address.new(city: "London"))

moved = p.with(home: p.home.with(city: "Berlin"))
p.home.city                     # still 'London'

# dry-struct equivalent: ImmutableStruct.new(...).new(city: "Berlin")
pitfalls: `with` copies the member references, not their contents: replacing a member is safe, but a mutable Array/Hash member is shared between the copy and the original.
Data classes forbid writers without freezing member objects - a shared mutable member still changes under both values, so deep immutability stays the caller's job (deep_freeze/`.freeze`).
`with` raises ArgumentError on an unknown keyword and does not exist before Ruby 3.3; on older runtimes the idiom silently degrades to `new(**to_h.merge(...))`, which rebuilds everything.
